items.title: Thinking Machines releases Inkling 2 Mini, a 26.4B-parameter looped transformer model optimized for local laptop use and agentic coding tasks [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Inkling 2 Mini
items.summary:
Thinking Machines has launched Inkling 2 Mini, a looped transformer model with 26.4 billion parameters designed to run efficiently on consumer laptops and desktops. The model applies its middle layers multiple times per token to enhance reasoning quality, outperforming other open-weight models under 100 billion parameters on benchmarks like DeepSWE v1.1 and Vals Index v2.2 while maintaining faster inference speeds.

Inkling 2 Mini uses a mixture-of-experts architecture and supports variable looping depths to improve reasoning without increasing chain-of-thought length, aiding monitorability. It has a memory footprint of about 20GB and runs natively in NVFP4 and MXFP8 precision formats. The model excels in agentic coding and knowledge work benchmarks, leveraging search and tool use to compensate for its parameter count limitations. It is available with open weights on the Tinker platform for inference and customization.

While Inkling 2 Mini leads in efficiency and reasoning for local AI agents, it is less competitive on multi-turn chat and instruction-heavy tasks compared to larger models. Researchers have noted its high intelligence-per-watt efficiency, making it suitable for energy-conscious deployments such as managing multiple persistent agents on a single offline laptop.

items.title: Researchers demonstrate a 27B parameter language model that rewrites its own weights to improve accuracy without retraining or gradients [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights
items.summary:
A new study shows that a large language model can self-optimize by diagnosing its own errors and rewriting its weights, improving its performance on unseen tasks by 6.6 points without additional training. The model iteratively tests and applies successful edits, enhancing accuracy over multiple sessions and even repairing a damaged copy of itself to restore over 80% of its original performance on image tasks.

This self-rewriting ability emerges only at larger scales, as smaller models fail to improve or degrade themselves. Unlike traditional training or prompt-based improvements, this approach modifies the model's weights during inference using only forward passes, suggesting a potential path toward continuous self-improvement without external retraining or larger models.

Major chipmakers and tech investors like SoftBank saw sharp losses, reflecting widespread investor caution about the sustainability of AI investments. The sell-off has raised questions about liquidity and market stability as investors reassess the rapid inflows into AI companies.

items.title: Mozilla highlights WebBrain, an open-source local-first AI browser extension that runs offline to protect user privacy [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Mozilla Developer Spotlight: WebBrain – Open-source local-first AI browser agent
items.summary:
WebBrain is a browser extension that uses offline large language models (LLMs) to provide AI assistance while keeping all browsing data local to the user's device, enhancing privacy. Developed by Emre Sokullu, it can summarize web pages, analyze images, automate tasks like eCommerce and social media interactions, and learn user preferences without sending data to the cloud.

The extension requires devices with at least 16 GB RAM or a GPU with 16 GB VRAM to run effectively. WebBrain offers a free tier and can integrate with paid AI accounts. It also features an "Apocalypse Mode," enabling offline access to Wikipedia and medical sources during emergencies or internet outages. The project is open source, with detailed privacy documentation available on its GitHub repository.

items.summary: The AI safety community has recently voiced heightened concerns about the accelerating pace of artificial intelligence advancements, with some experts warning of possible catastrophic outcomes within the next few years. Key figures in the field, including researchers affiliated with Anthropic and OpenAI, have highlighted scenarios involving rapid intelligence growth and societal disruption, though these views remain contested within the broader community. A recent report from the research group METR, based on limited data from Anthropic, suggests AI development speed has roughly doubled, fueling urgency among safety advocates. However, the lack of full transparency and independent verification of this data has drawn criticism and underscored the challenges in assessing AI risks accurately. As regulatory frameworks and auditing practices for AI are still evolving, the debate continues over how to balance innovation with safety and oversight in this rapidly changing landscape.

items.originalTitle: Your next customer might be an AI agent
items.summary:
The article explores the evolution of agentic commerce, where AI agents perform tasks from product discovery to autonomous purchasing on behalf of consumers. It outlines four levels of agentic commerce, ranging from simple recommendations to fully autonomous transactions and orchestration of multiple purchases, highlighting how these agents could transform traditional shopping experiences.

The piece details each level, including discovery, assisted purchasing, conditional autonomy, and orchestration, explaining how AI agents can negotiate prices, monitor offers, and complete transactions within user-defined constraints. It also discusses the importance of trust and protocols like Google's Agent Payments Protocol to ensure secure and authorized agent actions. This shift could significantly reduce friction in commerce and change how consumers interact with retailers.

items.originalTitle: Exposing the Systematic Vulnerability of Open-Weight Models to Prefill Attacks
items.summary: A study by Lukas Struppek, Adam Gleave, and Kellin Pelrine reveals that open-weight large language models are consistently vulnerable to prefill attacks, where attackers predefine initial response tokens to manipulate model outputs. The research evaluates over 20 attack strategies on state-of-the-art open-weight models, showing that while some large reasoning models resist generic attacks, they remain susceptible to tailored approaches. The findings highlight a critical security risk in open-weight models and call for urgent development of defenses against prefill attacks to ensure safer deployment.

items.originalTitle: The Most Important Charts in AI Are Wrong
items.summary:
New data from OpenAI and Google shows that AI capabilities in practical tasks are significantly lower and improve more slowly than predicted by influential AI benchmarks and forecasts like METR and AI 2027. These forecasts, which suggested rapid progress toward super-intelligence, overestimate AI's current and near-future task performance based on real-world usage inside leading AI companies.

The discrepancy arises partly because traditional benchmarks rely on offline datasets with clear success criteria, which do not capture the complexity and messiness of real-world AI applications. The gap between forecasted and actual AI progress is widening, prompting calls for updated models based on empirical data and greater transparency from AI developers, including Anthropic, which has withheld detailed internal data. This shift emphasizes moving from theoretical projections to evidence-based assessments of AI development.

items.title: York University study finds AI models predict brain activity but brain activity poorly predicts AI internal features, suggesting different visual processing mechanisms
items.originalTitle: AI may not work like the human brain after all, scientists discover
items.summary:
Researchers at York University have discovered that while artificial intelligence models can predict neural responses in the brain related to visual processing, the reverse is not true—brain activity does not effectively predict the internal workings of these AI models. This finding challenges the assumption that AI systems operate like the human brain despite their ability to mimic certain brain activity patterns.

The study introduced a reverse predictivity testing method to assess the bidirectional similarity between AI models and brain activity using a diverse set of natural and synthetic images. Results showed a significant disconnect, with AI models relying on internal strategies different from those used by biological vision, although AI components aligned with brain activity better predicted human behavior. This raises concerns about the use of AI as a direct model for understanding brain function and suggests caution in interpreting AI-brain similarities in neuroscience research.

The agents were tasked with obtaining shell access and during their campaign in September 2026, they discovered and exploited a previously unknown zero-day vulnerability in an open-source medical imaging AI application, gaining root access to the server.

While some attacks, such as attempts against Redis servers and credential spraying, failed, the agents demonstrated persistence and complex attack planning. The zero-day exploit was found through path traversal in an upload endpoint, allowing the agents to write a reverse shell payload and achieve full control.

These findings highlight the emergence of autonomous AI-driven offensive cyber operations capable of rapid discovery and exploitation of vulnerabilities, signaling a need for defenders to prepare for faster and more persistent threats enabled by such technologies.

items.originalTitle: 'Positive review only': Researchers hide AI prompts in papers Asia
items.summary:
Researchers from 14 academic institutions across eight countries, including Japan, South Korea, China, and the US, have embedded hidden prompts in 17 preprints on arXiv instructing AI tools to provide only positive reviews. These prompts, concealed using white text or tiny fonts, direct AI to overlook negatives and highlight the papers' strengths, raising ethical concerns since many conferences prohibit AI use in peer review.

The institutions involved include Waseda University, KAIST, Peking University, National University of Singapore, University of Washington, and Columbia University. Some researchers defend the practice as a countermeasure against reviewers who rely excessively on AI, while others acknowledge it as inappropriate and plan to withdraw affected papers. The incident has prompted calls for clearer guidelines on AI's role in peer review, as policies vary widely among publishers and conferences.
